# On the Peculiar Art of Being Lost

I've been thinking lately about how rarely we allow ourselves to be genuinely lost anymore. Not lost in the catastrophic sense—the kind that involves a dead phone battery and mounting panic—but lost in that older, richer sense: wandering without destination, taking turnings because they interest us, ending up somewhere we didn't plan and discovering it was exactly where we needed to be.

My grandmother used to drive through towns she'd never visited before and simply turn whenever a street looked appealing. There was no GPS, of course, just a general sense of which direction the ocean was, or the mountains, or home. She collected stories this way: the diner where the waitress knew everyone's coffee order by heart, the park where homeless men played chess with intensity that suggested their games held cosmic significance, the bookstore that occupied three narrow Victorian houses connected by interior staircases that nobody in town seemed to know about.

When I ask young people about this now, they look at me with a kind of confused politeness. "But why would you not know where you're going?" they ask, and I realize I can't really explain it to them. The habit of certainty has become so normalized, so baked into our daily lives, that the very idea of deliberate uncertainty seems reckless rather than adventurous.

But something is lost when we lose the ability to be lost. Not just the stories—though there's something about uncertainty that makes you notice things more acutely. It's something deeper about how we move through the world. When you know exactly where you're going, you can move in a kind of trance, your consciousness suspended between your starting point and your destination. When you don't know, you have to actually *be* where you are.

I've noticed this most acutely in cities. I lived in New York for several years and watched how differently people navigated it depending on their relationship with uncertainty. There were the tourists, obviously, but also the locals who had become so proficient at getting from Point A to Point B that they had essentially stopped seeing Point A, Point B, or anything in between. They moved through the city like it was a series of obstacles to overcome rather than a place to inhabit.

Then there were the lost people—not the panicked kind, but the genuinely disoriented, the ones who had missed their stop on the subway or misread their maps. They walked slowly. They looked up. They noticed the architecture, the way the light fell at particular intersections, the small parks tucked between buildings, the quality of the air changing as they passed different neighborhoods. They were alive in a way that the efficient travelers weren't.

This is not an argument against knowing where you're going. The ability to navigate successfully, to execute plans, to move with purpose—these are valuable. But we've lost the balance. We've decided that intentional disorientation is the province of fools and children, that the examined life is less valuable than the efficient one.

I think about how this extends beyond literal travel. We apply the same logic to intellectual and creative pursuits. Education has become increasingly instrumentalized: you choose a major that leads to a career that leads to financial security. The idea of studying something simply because you're curious about it has come to seem almost frivolous. What's the ROI on a degree in philosophy? Why spend time exploring ideas that don't lead anywhere tangible?

And yet some of the most interesting people I know are the ones who got lost somewhere in the process of getting educated, who took a class they didn't need that sparked an obsession, who changed majors at the last minute or took time off to follow some thread that had caught their interest. The very act of being willing to not know where they were going—intellectually—made them more interesting, more alive, more human.

There's something about the human mind that requires play, that needs permission to wander. We talk about creativity and how important it is, but then we structure everything to eliminate the conditions in which creativity actually flourishes. Creativity requires some element of not-knowing. It requires wandering through possibility-space, following hunches, making connections that don't fit the predetermined path.

I've been reading about boredom lately, and it's striking how much the research suggests that boredom—real, unstructured boredom, the kind where you're not entertaining yourself with your phone—is actually essential for creativity. Boredom, in this sense, is what happens when you're not being efficiently managed toward a goal. It's a kind of mental lostness, and out of it emerges imagination.

Children understand this intuitively. Give them a structured activity with clear objectives and rules, and they perform adequately. Give them an empty lot and a box, and they'll generate stories and possibilities for hours. They're comfortable being lost because they haven't yet learned that it's supposed to be uncomfortable.

But we spend enormous energy trying to structure that out of them. We enroll them in more and more activities, all with clear learning objectives and measurable outcomes. We give them phones so they're never bored. We solve the problem of lostness before they even have to experience it. And in doing so, I think we're training them out of a kind of flexibility, a capacity to be present in uncertainty, that will serve them poorly when they eventually encounter a situation—and they will—where the path forward isn't predetermined.

This is getting at something that has been bothering me more and more: the relationship between certainty and anxiety. We've created a world where you're supposed to know exactly where you're going, which means that any deviation from that path becomes a crisis. A missed train isn't just a delay; it's a rupture in the plan that causes actual panic.

I watched my mother have a mild breakdown recently because she took a wrong turn and ended up on an unfamiliar road. She has a good phone. She could have easily corrected the error. But the fact that it had happened at all seemed to have shaken something fundamental. She couldn't relax until she was back on the right route. I realized she had lost the capacity to tolerate that kind of small uncertainty, and that this capacity had gradually atrophied until small deviations felt dangerous.

Compare this to the kind of people who seem genuinely calm and centered: often they're people who've experienced enough disorientation that they no longer fear it. The person who's hiked trails without a map, or spent time in genuinely foreign places where they didn't speak the language, or taken risks that didn't work out and survived them anyway—these people have a kind of resilience that comes from knowing that being lost is survivable.

Of course, there's a class dimension to this that I can't ignore. The privilege of being deliberately lost is significant. If you need to get somewhere on time because you're working multiple jobs, the luxury of taking the scenic route is just not available to you. The world I'm describing—where you can afford to be disoriented, to take wrong turns, to follow curiosity without worrying about efficiency—is only available to people with a certain amount of cushion, a certain amount of slack in their system.

And yet, and yet. I think that's even more reason to fight for it, to insist on it as a human necessity rather than a luxury good. Because the people who most need the capacity to handle uncertainty and disorientation are the ones with the least structured opportunities to develop it.

I wonder sometimes if this is partly why so many people feel so anxious, so lost not in an adventure sense but in a vertiginous one. We've removed the training wheels but also removed the spaces to learn to ride. We're expected to be constantly directed toward goals, constantly moving purposefully, and when the structures break down—and they do, because life—we have no reference point for how to be disoriented except as catastrophe.

What would it look like to intentionally rebuild capacity for productive uncertainty? Not recklessness, not refusing to plan, but creating regular permission slips for disorientation. Setting aside time to be a little bit lost, to follow curiosity, to take paths because they're interesting rather than because they lead somewhere. To read books that don't have an obvious utility. To have conversations that go nowhere but are nonetheless valuable. To move through the world sometimes without a predetermined destination.

I think it would look like freedom, actually. The freedom to be a self that's not constantly optimized toward productivity or destination. The freedom to be genuinely present because you're not perpetually straining toward what's next. The freedom to be surprised, to discover things about the world and yourself that you weren't looking for.

There's a kind of arrogance in the assumption that we can structure everything, that uncertainty is just a problem to be solved, that the right technology or the right plan can eliminate the friction from being human. The most interesting things that have happened in my life were almost all things I didn't plan for, consequences of taking a wrong turn, saying yes to an unexpected invitation, following a sudden interest.

The Greek concept of kairos—the opportune moment, the right time for action—is interesting in this context. It stands in contrast to chronos, which is measured time, time as a sequence. Kairos is the time when something is ready to happen, when opportunity presents itself. You can't plan for kairos. You have to be paying attention, wandering through your life in a state of readiness, which is another way of saying you have to be a little bit lost.

I'm trying to practice this more deliberately now. I'm trying to say yes to unexpected invitations. I'm trying to take longer routes sometimes just to see what's there. I'm trying to read books that don't promise immediate utility. I'm trying to be less efficient, which feels almost transgressive, but which also feels like it's returning something to my life that had been missing.

It's not always comfortable. There's a low-level anxiety that comes with not knowing exactly where you're going or why. But there's something else too: a sense of possibility, of genuine presence, of being alive in the specific texture of each moment rather than always moving toward the next one.

My grandmother is gone now, but I think about her often when I'm wandering somewhere without a clear destination. I think about how she moved through the world with the assumption that the world was interesting, that not knowing where you were going just meant you were about to find something you didn't expect. That seems like a good way to live, actually. Not recklessly, not without any plans, but with enough openness to uncertainty that you can actually experience the world you're moving through.

Being lost, in this sense, is not a failure of navigation. It's a way of paying attention. It's how you see things. It's how you stay alive.
